title: S.W.A.T.
full_review:
An elite Los Angeles law enforcement unit must bring a notorious international criminal to justice in the loud and lackluster "S.W.A.T." (Columbia). In reality, the only person who should be brought up on charges is Clark Johnson, for impersonating a film director in what amounts to essentially a mindless B-movie guns-'n'-ammo fest with an A-movie price tag. Based on the popular 1970s TV series of the same name, "S.W.A.T." is an acronym which stands for "Special Weapons And Tactics" -- or, in this film's case, "Sloppily Written Action Twaddle." The story centers on Jim Street (Colin Farrell), a former team member relegated to desk duty following a controversial hostage standoff during which he and his partner, Brian Gamble (Jeremy Renner), disobeyed direct orders, an act which consequently resulted in loose-cannon Gamble getting tossed off the force altogether.

Street gets a chance at redemption when veteran commander Dan "Hondo" Harrelson (Samuel L. Jackson) arrives on the scene and is assigned to recruit five battle-tested cops in order to form a new S.W.A.T. division. Hondo sets his scope on Street, identifying with his brand of maverick moxie. Filling out the ranks are "Deke" (James Todd Smith, aka LL Cool J), Boxer (Brian Van Holt), McCabe (Josh Charles) and, in a lame attempt to give the team a feminist twist, laconic Latina Chris Sanchez (Michelle Rodriguez).

About 40 wasted minutes into the film, Johnson should have put out an all-points-bulletin for a missing plot. Mercifully, after several protracted training sequences, a sketchy story begins to emerge involving a French crime boss, Alex Montel (Olivier Martinez), who, after being nabbed for a moving violation, audaciously offers a kingpin's ransom to anyone who can spring him from police custody before he is handed over to the Feds. In a rare exhibition of racial harmony, Bloods and Crips join forces together with Asian and Hispanic gang-bangers in order to free Montel and collect the $100 million bounty. Downtown L.A. erupts into a war-zone as Hondo's crew is called in to escort the foie-gras felon to the pen.

Regrettably, the film is little more than a testosterone-driven symphony of crescendos and pauses, wringing dry the audience's already depleted adrenal glands. In fact, the final 40 minutes of the film is barely distinguishable from countless other tedious shoot 'em ups and mind-numbing crash-and-smash sequences churned out and force fed to moviegoers throughout the summer.

To its credit, the film refrains from excessive gore and clearly delineates between "good guys" and "bad guys," but any such moral distinctions are Pyrrhic victories given the flick's misguided overall treatment of violence as entertainment.

The movie's tagline, "Even cops dial 911," suggests that during certain crises even police need help. Perhaps it would have paid dividends if the screenwriter had at some point picked up the phone and dialed "emergency" as well, given his apparent shabby grasp of character and narrative development. The cardboard team members are uniformly two-dimensional, distinguished only by their skin tone and facial hair -- thank goodness that their names are printed on their flak vests, or, in Gamble's case, tattooed on his forearm.

Midway through, Montel shouts, "I'll give a hundred million dollars to anyone who can get me out of here." Viewers subjected to this clunker may contemplate making a similar deal. This movie doesn't need S.W.A.T.; it is fodder for the bomb-squad.

Due to much violence, some profanity and some crude sexual language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
